notes:
I've put together notes for John 9:21–41, but the research is incomplete. The full Enduring Word and Pulpit Commentary pages were cut off before verse 21, so most of what follows comes from shorter search excerpts. I found nothing usable from Lutheran, Orthodox, Pentecostal-denominational, bibleodyssey.org or prosperity/word-of-faith sources, and nothing at all on v. 30, so those are left out.

---

**v. 21**
- The parents probably had no doubt about the healing, but they hadn't seen it happen, so their word wouldn't count as legal evidence. "He is of age" means he was old enough to testify, which among Jews was thirteen (Barnes). It appears that they had themselves no doubt, but they were not eye-witnesses, and could not be therefore legal evidence. He is of age - He is of sufficient age to give testimony. Among the Jews this age was fixed at thirteen years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-22.htm
- Another commentator on the same page says the parents dodged the truth when they claimed not to know who opened his eyes, because they were afraid. They prevaricated, however, in saying they "knew not who had opened his eyes," for "they feared the Jews," https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-22.htm

**vv. 22–23**
- Ellicott notes that the word translated "agreed" appears only twice more in the New Testament: It expresses the covenant made with Judas, in Luke 22:5, and the agreement of the Jews to kill Paul, in Acts 23:20. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-22.htm
- Barnes describes two levels of excommunication. The lighter one shut a man out of the synagogue for 30 days. The heavier one was a solemn exclusion forever from the worship of the synagogue, attended with awful maledictions and curses, and an exclusion from all contact with the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-22.htm
- Gill also distinguishes a temporary ban ("Niddui") from a full curse that cut a person off from the whole Jewish people ("Cherem"), and says this struck great terror in the minds of the people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-22.htm
- **Sources disagree on which ban is meant.** One commentary on the page (heading cut off; the wording suggests the Cambridge Bible) lists three kinds and says this passage probably refer[s] to the first and mildest kind of anathema. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-22.htm The Bible Hub Study Bible instead identifies it as "herem", a form of excommunication that severed individuals from the religious and social life of the Jewish community. https://biblehub.com/study/john/9-22.htm
- The Greek word for "put out of the synagogue" appears only in John's Gospel, here and in 12:42 and 16:2 (Vincent). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-22.htm
- Bengel says the parents were so afraid that they left their son alone in the danger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-22.htm
- Constable: "For a Jew to be put out of the synagogue meant that he was ostracized by everyone." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-22.html
- *Reformed application (Calvin):* people who are not subject to Christ have no lawful power to excommunicate. Believers needn't fear being thrown out of such assemblies, since Christ, who is our life and salvation, is banished from it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-22.html
- Matthew Henry warns that church discipline has often been turned against itself, and ecclesiastical censures have been made to serve a carnal secular interest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/john/9.htm

**vv. 24–25**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says the man's plain testimony outweighs the Pharisees' clever arguments. He didn't know everything about Jesus, but he knew what Jesus had done for him, and at that moment, it was an irrefutable argument. They could not argue against what Jesus did in this man's life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Pulpit Commentary: the Jews reason from prejudices they already hold, while the man answers with "invincible conviction". It reads "Now I see!" as an indication of present experience, and an earnest of future development. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/john-9.html

**vv. 26–27**
- Guzik sees simple wisdom in the man's reply: If they kept asking the same question, they would keep hearing the same answer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- In Guzik's list of the man's growing titles for Jesus, verse 27 is where Jesus becomes his master and he becomes His disciple. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/john/john-9.cfm

**vv. 28–29**
- Guzik says the leaders show their pride and their prejudiced contempt for Jesus, calling Him "this fellow". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Precept Austin notes that "spoken" is in the Greek perfect tense: what God said to Moses still stands on record. The leaders were right that God did speak to Moses. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-9-commentary

**v. 31: commentators really do disagree here**
- Ellicott sets out the man's reasoning in three steps: God hears only those who worship Him and do His will; God clearly heard this Man, since only divine power could do such a miracle; so this Man is not a sinner but is from God. https://biblehub.com/john/9-31.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: God does not hear sinners in the sense of giving them special miraculous approval. The blind beggar has learned the deepest truth of the Divine revelation about the conditions of acceptable prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-31.htm
- Poole (Puritan): God has made no covenant promise to hear sinners, yet out of goodness He may still hear them, as He heard Ahab. Here the point is narrower: God does not give notorious sinners the power to work miracles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-31.htm
- Gill (Baptist): everyone is a sinner, and God hears every sinner who repents. "Sinners" here means people in whom sin reigns, especially impostors. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html
- **Is the man stating Bible truth, or just a common belief? Teachers split.**
  - *Calvin (Reformed)* says it is a mistake to read this as the man merely repeating popular opinion. It is the uniform doctrine of Scripture, that God does not listen to any but those who call upon him with truth and sincerity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html
  - *Barnes (Presbyterian)* says the verse has nothing to do with sinners praying for salvation. It was the mere opinion of this man, in accordance with the common sentiment of the Jews, and there is no evidence that he was inspired. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html
  - *Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel)* agrees with Barnes: the verse can't support a doctrine that God ignores sinners' prayers, because if God didn't hear sinners when they pray, none of us would be saved. God does hear sinners, and that's part of the grace and the mercy of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html
  - *Coffman (Restoration Movement, Arminian)* takes "hearing" to mean God empowering a person to do a miracle. He points out that God heard Cornelius before his conversion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html
  - *Adam Clarke (Methodist)* thinks "sinners" here means heathens, set against a worshipper of the true God. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/john/9-31.html He also lists cases where God does not hear, such as when people wish to be saved, and yet abide in their sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html
  - *Benson (Methodist)* applies it to impenitent sinners and to God helping them work miracles. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html
  - *GotQuestions:* In context, though, John 9:31 is saying that God does not perform miracles through an unbeliever. https://www.gotquestions.org/unbeliever-prayer.html
  - *Catholic (Haydock):* God does not hear sinners in such a particular way as to work miracles in favour of them and their doctrine. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html

**vv. 32–33**
- Guzik says this is the first time in the Bible that anyone born blind is healed, and that opening blind eyes is a work of the LORD (Ps 146:8) and of the Messiah (Isa 35:5). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the miracle proves He is not a wicked man, and more than that, that He is of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-31.html

**v. 34**
- Pulpit Commentary: the leaders physically pushed him out of the place where they were sitting. Scripture doesn't say they formally excommunicated him then and there, though his confession made him liable to the ban announced in v. 22. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/john/9.htm
- Poole thinks "cast out" probably means excommunication. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/9-35.htm
- Kelly links this to John 10:3, where the shepherd "leads out" his own sheep, and says Christ gives their wicked act His own interpretation, according to divine counsels. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-22.html

**v. 35**
- *Which title did Jesus use?* Older translations (KJV, NKJV) read "Son of God"; most modern ones read "Son of Man".
  - Ellicott admits most of the best manuscripts have "Son of Man". But he says "Son of God" is certainly as old as the second century, and seems to supply the sense which the context requires. https://biblehub.com/john/9-35.htm
  - Constable: Some early manuscripts and modern translations have "Son of God," but "Son of Man" has the better support. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-35.html
  - Steven Cole: "Son of Man" is almost certainly the original text. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-53-blind-see-seeing-are-blind-john-935-41
  - Guzik: Both terms point to God's Messiah, the One who should be believed and trusted. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/john/john-9.cfm
- Jesus takes the first step: the man had little light, so Jesus sought him out with more revelation to bring him to full faith (Constable). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-35.html
- Matthew Henry: believing on the Son of God is the great thing God now asks of us, and by this we must stand or fall for ever. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_009.cfm

**vv. 36–37**
- D. A. Carson (quoted by Precept Austin) says Jesus invites the man to trust Him as the One who reveals God. Cole answers "Who is the Son of Man?" with: the eternal Word who became flesh, died for sins, rose, and will judge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-9-commentary
- Expositor's Dictionary of Texts: the Greek word for "speaking" suggests frank, friendly conversation, such as two friends might have with one another. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/edt/john-9.html

**v. 38**
- NET Bible note (quoted by Precept Austin): the note assumes 9:38–39a is genuine, which shows there is a manuscript question here. If it is, the man's worship would connote its full sense: This was something due God alone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-9-commentary
- Guzik: by accepting worship, Jesus shows both that He is God and that He welcomes people religious institutions reject. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/
- Pulpit Commentary: the confession is "prompt, unhesitating, and enduring". They who believe in Christ for salvation will be sure to worship him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/john-9.html
- Commentators trace the man's growing understanding: "a man" (v. 11), "a prophet" (v. 17), "from God" (v. 33), and finally "Lord" or "Son of God" (vv. 35–38). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-9/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/9-35.html
- Matthew Henry adds that we never read of this man again, but he very likely became a constant follower of Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_009.cfm

**v. 39**
- Guzik: Jesus divides humanity. Our choice does not determine who Jesus is; it determines who we are. https://enduringword.com/why-jesus-came/
- Tasker (quoted by Precept Austin): the last three verses show the whole story is an acted parable of faith and unbelief, and therefore of judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-9-commentary
- Pulpit Commentary applies "those who see may become blind" to people who are "wise in our own eyes, and prudent in our own sight." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/john-9.html
- Expositor's Dictionary of Texts: the blind man came to believe, while the Pharisees hardened in unbelief. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/edt/john-9.html

**vv. 40–41**
- Pulpit Commentary: the Pharisees are the opposite of the "not-seeing"; they are self-satisfied and will not come to the Light. Their sin will remain until you fully admit the great principle and reason, the motive and characteristics, of my mission. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/john-9.html
- Precept Austin (writer not named in the excerpt): people who know they are spiritually blind will quickly turn to the Saviour. "Your sin remaineth" as long as you walk in your fancied light. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-9-commentary
- Precept Austin also notes the leaders were blind to their own sin, so they stayed guilty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/what-does-it-mean-to-abide
- Matthew Henry, in his John 9 notes (I couldn't confirm which verse this is attached to), says nothing shields a corrupt heart from conviction more than a high opinion others have of it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_009.cfm

**Catholic and early Church readings (whole passage)**
- Augustine reads the blind man as a picture of the whole human race, blinded through Adam's sin. If evil has so taken root within us, every man is born mentally blind. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701044.htm In his next sermon (Tractate 45) he says John 10 continues straight on from vv. 39–40. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1701045.htm
- Catholic Answers reads the healing as teaching about baptism, and the persistent unbelief in the story as a sign of ongoing blindness to God's work in Christ. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/baptism-and-the-cure-for-blindness
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that John 9 was the Gospel reading at the "great scrutiny" of people preparing for baptism. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/03430b.htm
